client: I got a rejection letter from my dream university last week, and honestly it's been messing with my head ever since. I keep replaying all the things I could have done differently, like maybe I should have worked harder or been more impressive somehow. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It takes real courage to reach out even when part of you isn't sure it'll help, and I'm glad you did. That loop of replaying "what I could have done differently" sounds exhausting — like your mind is trying to solve a problem that may not actually have a clean solution. I'm curious: when you imagine that "more impressive" version of yourself who got in, what does that person have that you feel you're missing right now?

client: I guess that person is just... more sure of themselves, you know? Like they walk into a room and they don't second-guess every single thing they say or do. I feel like I'm always waiting to become that version of me, and it's starting to feel like maybe I never actually will.
therapist: There's something quietly painful in what you just shared — this sense of waiting to become yourself, like the "real you" is always just out of reach. I want to gently reflect something back: the person who kept going after a painful rejection, who reached out even while doubting it would help — that actually takes a kind of quiet confidence, even if it doesn't feel that way from the inside. What do you think it would mean for your life if that more certain version of you never arrived — would that truly mean you couldn't have the things that matter to you?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but it also feels a little too neat, you know? Like, sure, I reached out, but I did it half-convinced it was pointless, so I'm not sure that counts as confidence so much as just... desperation. And honestly, the idea that I might never feel more certain or solid in myself — that's not reassuring, that's actually kind of terrifying to sit with.
therapist: You're right to push back on that — I don't want to offer you something that feels like a shortcut past real pain, and the fear you're naming, that you might always feel this unsteady, deserves to be taken seriously rather than smoothed over. What I notice though is that you're making a very permanent-sounding conclusion ("I'll never feel solid") from a moment when you're still raw from a real loss, which is exactly when our minds tend to present their harshest verdicts as facts. I'm wondering — has there ever been a time in your life, even briefly, where you felt a little more grounded in yourself, and what was different about that moment?

client: I have to think about that for a second, because my first instinct is to say no, never, but that's probably not actually true. There was a period maybe three years ago when I had a close group of friends nearby and I felt like I mattered to people, like I wasn't just waiting for someone to notice I existed. But then people moved away and that fell apart, and I guess what I'm realizing is that the groundedness wasn't really coming from inside me, it was coming from them, so I don't know how much that even counts.
therapist: That memory clearly means something real — you did feel grounded once, and that matters, even if you're now questioning the source of it. I'd gently challenge the idea that it "doesn't count" though, because needing other people to feel solid isn't a flaw or a weakness — it's actually deeply human, and most of us build our sense of self partly through connection. What's interesting to explore is whether that period taught you anything about *what you need* to feel like you matter, rather than seeing it as proof that you can't generate that feeling yourself — what do you think it was about those friendships specifically that made you feel seen?

client: I guess... what made those friendships feel different was that they actually remembered things about me, like small details I'd mentioned weeks earlier, and it made me feel like I existed in someone's mind even when I wasn't around. But I keep coming back to this fear that if I needed them that much, then losing them hit so hard because I never really had anything solid inside myself to fall back on. It's like the loneliness I feel now isn't just about missing them, it's about not trusting that I'm worth remembering to anyone anymore.
therapist: What you just described — wanting to exist in someone's mind even when you're not in the room — is one of the most tender and human needs there is, and it makes complete sense that losing that hit you so deeply. But I want to sit with something you said: you're interpreting needing those friendships as evidence that you're empty inside, but it could just as easily be evidence that you know, quite precisely, what meaningful connection feels like — which is actually a kind of self-knowledge. I'm curious, when you imagine someone worth remembering, what qualities come to mind — and do you ever find yourself applying that same measure to how you see yourself?

client: That's... a strange question to sit with, because when I think about someone worth remembering, I think of people who make others feel seen, who show up consistently, who leave some kind of mark on the world around them. And honestly, when I try to apply that to myself, there's this immediate wall that comes up — like the question doesn't even compute, like I'm not a candidate for that kind of assessment. I want to believe what you're saying about self-knowledge, but it feels more like I just know what I'm missing rather than knowing something valuable about myself.
therapist: That wall you described — where the question "doesn't even compute" for you — is actually really important, because it's not a neutral observation, it's a rule your mind has quietly installed that says you're exempt from being assessed as worthwhile. And here's what strikes me: you described someone worth remembering as a person who makes others feel seen — and earlier you told me about friendships where people remembered small details about *you*, which means someone, at some point, experienced you as exactly that kind of person. I'm wondering what it would take for you to even provisionally consider that their experience of you might be as valid as the story you tell about yourself?

client: That's... a hard thing to sit with, because part of me wants to just dismiss it and say those people were wrong about me, or they were seeing something that wasn't really there. Like maybe they were just being kind, or they weren't paying close enough attention. I know that sounds like I'm working really hard to protect this story I have about myself, and I can almost see that I'm doing it, but it doesn't make it any easier to stop.
therapist: The fact that you can almost see yourself doing it — discarding evidence that doesn't fit, finding reasons why the people who valued you were simply mistaken — that's actually a significant moment of awareness, and it's worth pausing on. What you're describing is a belief that's working very hard to survive, one that keeps finding new ways to disqualify anything that threatens it, which tells me it's been protecting you from something for a long time. I'm curious — what do you think that story about yourself has been keeping you safe from, if you had to guess?

client: That's a hard question to sit with, honestly. I think maybe... if I let myself believe I actually matter to people, and then they leave anyway, that would be so much worse than just assuming they never really cared in the first place. It's like the story keeps me from getting blindsided — if I already expect to be alone, then being alone doesn't get to hurt me the same way.
therapist: You just named something really profound — this belief isn't really about what you deserve, it's a shield you built after real loss, a way of getting ahead of the pain before it can ambush you. And it makes complete sense that it felt necessary, because the hurt of losing those friendships was real. But I want to gently ask: how much living has that shield been costing you — the connections you might not have reached for, the moments you couldn't let yourself fully have — and is the protection it offers actually worth that price?

client: That question kind of lands somewhere uncomfortable, honestly. Because when I actually think about it, yeah, I've probably pulled back from people more times than I can count, just... preemptively, before they could leave first. But admitting that the shield costs something feels almost more threatening than just keeping it up, because at least the loneliness I have now is predictable.
therapist: There's something quietly brave in what you just said — acknowledging that the predictability of loneliness has become its own kind of comfort, even as part of you recognizes the cost. What strikes me is that you came here today, to a conversation you half-expected to be pointless, which means some part of you is already testing whether the shield is still serving you — even if another part is gripping it tightly. I'm wondering, if the loneliness you have now isn't actually safe so much as just *familiar*, what might feel like a small enough risk to take with another person that wouldn't feel like betting everything?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to agree with it, but then I immediately think of all the times I've tried to let someone in a little and it just... didn't go the way I hoped. Like, even small risks have backfired on me, so I'm not sure "small" actually exists when it comes to this stuff. It's not that I don't want connection, it's that I've kind of lost faith that I'm someone people actually want to stay around.
therapist: The exhaustion in what you're describing is real — not dramatic or catastrophic, just this quiet, worn-down sense that trying has repeatedly led to the same hurt, and at some point the math stops making sense. I want to acknowledge that your past experiences aren't nothing, they're real data, but I also notice that "people don't stay" has quietly expanded into "I'm someone people don't *want* to stay around" — which is a much bigger and more personal conclusion than the evidence actually proves. I'm curious, when those small risks didn't go the way you hoped, do you know what actually happened — did people consciously choose to leave you, or did life just move in ways that had little to do with your worth?
